Assessment: The tone of the April 29, 2020 FOMC statement is clearly cautious to negative given references to “sharp declines,” “surge in job losses,” and “considerable risks,” consistent with literature that pandemics elevate economic policy uncertainty and depress activity (pandemic → higher EPU). However, the Fed’s commitment to maintain rates at the effective lower bound and to deploy large-scale asset purchases, repos, and forward guidance reflects the playbook that research finds can anchor expectations and support transmission when inflation pressures are muted: inflation-forecast-based guidance (Svensson and Woodford, 2005), forward guidance and QE at the zero lower bound, and lender-of-last-resort principles in stressed markets (Bagehot-style liquidity, QE on Treasuries and agency MBS/CMBS). The emphasis on the symmetric 2 percent target and continuous monitoring of inflation expectations aligns with the inflation-targeting literature and expectations management frameworks. At the same time, evidence that QE’s real-growth effects can be limited and that liquidity traps constrain conventional policy keeps the overall tone negative despite the policy backstop. Netting these elements, the literature implies a slightly less negative sentiment than a pure reading of the outlook language would suggest.
